title: General Organic Chemistry

toc.title: 16.1 Tetravalency and catenation; classification; alkyl and aryl groups; functional groups and homologous series
16.2 IUPAC nomenclature of aliphatic compounds and isomerism
16.3 Bond fission, reactive intermediates and electronic effects

html:
Organic chemistry becomes manageable when you stop memorizing molecules one at a time and start reading their architecture. This chapter, worth about 3 questions, supplies that grammar: how carbon builds frameworks, how functional groups create families, how IUPAC names encode structure, how the same formula can represent different substances, and how electrons move when bonds break. These ideas decide nearly every mechanism in Chapters 17–20.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Carbon is tetravalent (four covalent bonds in neutral compounds) and strongly catenating: it links to itself in long chains, branches and rings, using single, double and triple bonds.
  • A functional group is the reactive atom or bond pattern defining a family. A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula, with successive members differing by CH₂ (14 mass units).
  • Remove H from an alkane to get an alkyl group (CH₃–, C₂H₅–). Remove H from an arene ring to get an aryl group (phenyl, C₆H₅–). Benzyl (C₆H₅CH₂–) is an aralkyl group, not an aryl group.
  • Count unsaturation before drawing isomers: degree of unsaturation = (2C + 2 + N - H - X)/2. Each ring or π bond contributes one; a triple bond contributes two. Oxygen does not enter the formula.
  • IUPAC naming: identify the senior functional group, choose the parent chain containing it (and maximum multiple bonds), number for lowest locants, then cite substituents alphabetically. Principal-group order for school work: acid > anhydride > ester > acid halide > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene > alkyne.
  • Structural isomers differ in connectivity: chain, position, functional-group, metamerism and tautomerism. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement: geometrical (cis/trans or E/Z) and optical isomerism are the school forms.
  • A carbon carrying four different groups is normally a stereogenic/chiral centre. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images; diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; a meso compound is achiral through internal symmetry despite stereocentres.
  • Homolysis splits a bond one electron to each atom and gives free radicals (fishhook arrows). Heterolysis sends both electrons to one atom and gives ions (double-headed curly arrow).
  • Carbocation stability generally increases methyl → 1° → 2° → 3°, and allylic/benzylic resonance gives extra stabilization. Simple alkyl carbanions show the reverse substitution trend. Free radicals broadly follow the carbocation order.
  • An electrophile accepts an electron pair; a nucleophile donates one. Carbocations are electrophiles, carbanions are nucleophiles.
  • The inductive effect is permanent σ-electron displacement toward a more electronegative atom/group (−I) or away from a donor (+I), weakening rapidly with distance. Resonance delocalizes π electrons or a lone pair over a conjugated system; the true structure is the hybrid, not a mixture flickering between drawings.

16.1 Tetravalency and catenation; classification; alkyl and aryl groups; functional groups and homologous series

Carbon has four valence electrons. In ordinary neutral organic compounds it shares four pairs of electrons, acquiring an octet while retaining a formal charge of zero. The four bonds may be arranged as four single bonds (tetrahedral, sp³), a double and two single bonds (trigonal planar, sp²), or a triple and one single bond/two double bonds (linear, sp). Charged carbon is the deliberate exception encountered later in the chapter: a carbocation has three bonds and an empty p orbital; a carbanion has three bonds and a lone pair.

Catenation is self-linking. It is exceptionally strong in carbon because the small atom forms strong C–C and C–H bonds and can also use p orbitals effectively in multiple bonds. Chains can branch, close into rings and support many functional groups. Silicon sits below carbon but forms weaker Si–Si bonds and much stronger Si–O bonds, so silicon chemistry flows toward silicate networks rather than an equally rich family of discrete Si-chain molecules.

Classification by carbon skeleton

Class Meaning Examples
Acyclic/aliphatic Open chain, straight or branched butane, 2-methylpropane, but-2-ene
Alicyclic Ring with broadly aliphatic behaviour cyclopropane, cyclohexane
Aromatic Cyclic conjugated system with special stability; benzene is the prototype benzene, phenol, aniline
Heterocyclic Ring contains an atom other than carbon furan (O in ring), pyridine (N in ring), thiophene (S in ring)

Compounds are also called saturated when the carbon framework has only single bonds and unsaturated when it contains a double bond, triple bond or ring equivalent. A ring creates the same hydrogen deficiency as one π bond even though cycloalkanes do not behave like alkenes in addition reactions.

Alkyl, aryl and related groups

A group obtained by removing one hydrogen from an alkane is an alkyl group, general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁–: methyl CH₃– (from methane), ethyl CH₃CH₂–, propyl CH₃CH₂CH₂– and propan-2-yl/isopropyl (CH₃)₂CH–. The atom bearing the free valence dictates names such as butan-2-yl. Carbon atoms are described as 1°, 2°, 3° or 4° according to how many other carbons are attached to them; alcohols and alkyl halides are similarly classified by the carbon carrying –OH or halogen.

An aryl group is formed by removing hydrogen directly from an aromatic ring. Phenyl is C₆H₅–; a methylphenyl group is tolyl. By contrast, C₆H₅CH₂– is benzyl: its free valence is on a saturated carbon next to the ring, making it an aralkyl group. This distinction matters in reactivity — a benzylic carbocation or radical is resonance-stabilized through the benzylic carbon, whereas a phenyl cation has its empty orbital in the ring plane and is very unstable. Two other pattern names recur: vinyl, CH₂=CH–, and allyl, CH₂=CH–CH₂–.

Functional groups and homologous series

The carbon skeleton is the stage; the functional group is usually where the action occurs. Members of one family therefore have similar chemistry, while physical properties change gradually as the hydrocarbon part grows.

Family Functional pattern Typical suffix/prefix Example
Alkane C–C, C–H only -ane propane
Alkene C=C -ene but-2-ene
Alkyne C≡C -yne pent-1-yne
Alcohol –OH on carbon -ol / hydroxy- propan-2-ol
Ether C–O–C alkoxy- (or ether name) methoxyethane
Aldehyde –CHO, terminal carbonyl -al / oxo- butanal
Ketone C–CO–C -one / oxo- pentan-3-one
Carboxylic acid –CO₂H -oic acid ethanoic acid
Ester –CO₂R alkyl …-oate methyl ethanoate
Acid halide –COX -oyl halide ethanoyl chloride
Amide –CONH₂ or substituted -amide ethanamide
Nitrile –C≡N -nitrile / cyano- propanenitrile
Amine –NH₂, –NHR, –NR₂ -amine / amino- ethanamine
Haloalkane C–F/Cl/Br/I halo- prefix 2-bromobutane
Nitro compound –NO₂ nitro- prefix nitroethane

A homologous series shares a general formula and functional group, has a common method of preparation, shows similar chemical reactions and displays gradual changes in melting point, boiling point, density and solubility. Adjacent members differ by –CH₂–. Useful general formulae for acyclic compounds are:

Series General formula Also fits
Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ —
Alkenes CₙH₂ₙ cycloalkanes
Alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ dienes, cycloalkenes
Monohydric alcohols/ethers CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O each other (functional isomers)
Aldehydes/ketones CₙH₂ₙO each other
Carboxylic acids/esters CₙH₂ₙO₂ each other

The degree of unsaturation (DU, also index of hydrogen deficiency) packs that comparison into one calculation:

\mathrm{DU}=\frac{2C+2+N-H-X}{2}

Halogen X is counted as hydrogen because both are monovalent; nitrogen adds one available hydrogen equivalent; divalent oxygen or sulfur does not alter the count. Benzene, C₆H₆, has DU = 4 — one ring plus three π bonds. DU never tells you which rings or π bonds are present, but it prevents impossible structures when enumerating isomers.

One formula, several lives

Problem. (a) Name (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ by IUPAC. (b) How many structural isomers does C₄H₉Br have? (c) Count σ and π bonds in CH₂=CH–C≡CH. Solution. (a) The longest chain holds five carbons with methyls at C2 and C4: 2,4-dimethylpentane. (b) The butyl skeleton offers four carbon environments — 1-bromo-, 2-bromo-, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: 4 isomers. (c) Vinylacetylene: four C–H σ bonds plus three C–C σ bonds = 7 σ; one double bond (1 π) plus one triple bond (2 π) = 3 π. Naming, counting and bookkeeping: the chapter's three exam verbs.

16.2 IUPAC nomenclature of aliphatic compounds and isomerism

A reliable four-pass naming routine

  1. Seniority pass. Find the principal functional group. It decides the suffix and should be included in the parent chain. The carbon of –COOH, –CHO or –CN is counted in the chain.
  2. Parent pass. Choose the longest continuous carbon chain containing the principal group; if there is a tie, prefer the chain with more multiple bonds, then more substituents.
  3. Numbering pass. Give the principal group the lowest possible locant. Next consider multiple bonds (for an enyne, the direction giving the lower locant to the first cited multiple bond, normally the alkene), then substituents as a set. If a set is tied, give the lower locant to the substituent cited first alphabetically.
  4. Assembly pass. Write substituents alphabetically with locants, ignoring multiplicative prefixes such as di- and tri- in alphabetization. Separate numbers with commas and numbers from words with hyphens: 3-ethyl-2,4-dimethylhexane.

When a lower-priority group is present it becomes a prefix: –OH is hydroxy- in the presence of a ketone, C=O is oxo- in the presence of a carboxylic acid, –NH₂ is amino-, –OR is alkoxy-, and halogens and –NO₂ are always prefixes in substitutive names. The parent chain name drops its terminal “e” before a vowel-starting suffix (pentan-2-one), while locants for unsaturation are placed immediately before -ene or -yne in modern format (but-2-ene, pent-1-yne).

Worked example 16.1 — name from the functional group outward

Problem. Name CH₃–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂–CHO and calculate its degree of unsaturation.

Solution. The aldehyde carbon must be C-1. Numbering from –CHO gives CHO = C1, CH₂ = C2, the substituted carbon = C3 and one methyl carbon completes a four-carbon butanal parent. Two additional methyl groups sit on C3, so the name is 3,3-dimethylbutanal. Its molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O. Hence DU = (2×6 + 2 − 12)/2 = 1, accounted for by C=O. The trap is to call the branched left-hand end “tert-butyl” and lose the requirement that the aldehyde carbon begins the parent chain.

Isomerism: same formula, different substance

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures and therefore at least some different properties. First ask whether atom-to-atom connections differ.

Structural (constitutional) isomerism

  • Chain isomerism: different carbon skeleton. C₄H₁₀ is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butane) or (CH₃)₃CH (2-methylpropane).
  • Position isomerism: same skeleton and functional group at a different position. Butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol; but-1-ene and but-2-ene.
  • Functional-group isomerism: different functional family. C₂H₆O is ethanol or methoxymethane; C₃H₆O is propanal or propanone.
  • Metamerism: different alkyl groups flank a polyvalent functional atom/group, as in ethoxyethane versus 1-methoxypropane (both C₄H₁₀O), or different substitution patterns around a ketone/secondary amine.
  • Tautomerism: rapidly interconverting structural isomers differing chiefly in position of a proton and a π bond, classically keto ⇌ enol. For simple ketones the keto form dominates overwhelmingly. Tautomers are distinct chemical species in equilibrium; resonance forms are not.

Useful alkane counts are C₄H₁₀ = 2, C₅H₁₂ = 3, C₆H₁₄ = 5 and C₇H₁₆ = 9 structural isomers. When counting substituted compounds, work skeleton by skeleton and mark symmetry-equivalent positions only once.

Stereoisomerism

Geometrical isomerism occurs when rotation is restricted — most often about C=C, but also in some rings. Each alkene carbon must carry two different substituents. In but-2-ene, cis has the two CH₃ groups on the same side and trans has them opposite. When all four substituents are different, cis/trans language has no clear reference pair; the E/Z system assigns priority to the two groups on each carbon by atomic number (Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules). High-priority groups on the same side give Z (zusammen, together); opposite sides give E (entgegen, opposite).

Optical isomerism is the school label for chirality at stereogenic centres. A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups lacks a symmetry plane through that arrangement and exists as two enantiomers. Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light by equal magnitudes in opposite directions and have identical melting points, boiling points and spectra in achiral environments. In a chiral environment — an enzyme pocket, receptor or chiral reagent — they can behave very differently, which is why drug stereochemistry matters. An equal mixture is a racemate and shows no net rotation (external compensation).

Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers; they generally have different physical properties and can be separated by ordinary crystallization or chromatography. A meso compound contains stereocentres but also an internal symmetry element, so the molecule is superposable on its mirror image and optically inactive (internal compensation). Thus “has two stereocentres” does not automatically mean “has four optically active forms”. Likewise, R/S is a configuration label assigned from viewing priorities; it does not by itself predict whether rotation is (+) or (−).

Two counting traps

Identical drawings produced by turning the paper over are not new isomers, and resonance forms are not isomers. Conversely, a chiral constitutional isomer represents a pair of enantiomers when a question asks for total stereoisomers. Always check whether the wording says structural, stereoisomers or optically active forms.

16.3 Bond fission, reactive intermediates and electronic effects

Homolytic and heterolytic fission

A covalent bond contains two electrons, so there are only two ways to divide them.

Feature Homolysis Heterolysis
Electron division One electron to each fragment Both electrons to one fragment
Products Two free radicals A cation and an anion
Arrow Single-barbed “fishhook” arrow Double-barbed curly arrow
Favoured by Heat, UV light, peroxides; nonpolar/gas-phase conditions Polar solvents and polarized bonds; stable ions
Typical chemistry Radical chain substitution, combustion Ionic substitution, elimination and addition mechanisms

For A–B heterolysis, the electron pair normally follows the more electronegative atom. In (CH₃)₃C–Br, heterolysis gives (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻; in aqueous solvent the ions are solvated and the tertiary carbocation is relatively stable. Homolysis of the same bond would give (CH₃)₃C• + Br•.

Worked example 16.2 — the same bond, two scripts

Problem. tert-Butyl bromide reacts rapidly with aqueous NaOH. Which fission begins the reaction, and which species attacks which?

Solution. Water is polar and Br is more electronegative than carbon, so heterolysis is favoured: the C–Br pair moves to Br, producing the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻. The carbocation is the electron-pair acceptor (electrophile). Hydroxide, with lone pairs, is the electron-pair donor (nucleophile) and attacks it. UV-driven homolysis to two radicals tells a different story and is not the script under aqueous ionic conditions.

Carbocations, carbanions and free radicals

Intermediate Carbon electrons/geometry Stability pattern Usual reactivity
Carbocation, C⁺ 6 valence electrons; usually planar sp² with empty p orbital 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl; allyl/benzyl resonance strongly stabilizing Electrophile; rearranges by hydride/alkyl shift if a better cation can form
Free radical, C• 7 valence electrons; near-planar at carbon; one unpaired electron Benzyl/allyl and 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (context dependent) Abstracts atoms, adds to π bonds, combines with another radical
Carbanion, C⁻ 8 valence electrons; lone pair, often pyramidal unless resonance flattens it Methyl > 1° > 2° > 3° for alkyl substitution; resonance and −I/−R groups stabilize Nucleophile and strong base

Why are tertiary carbocations and radicals relatively stable? Neighbouring C–H/C–C σ bonds can donate electron density into the empty or half-filled p orbital (hyperconjugation), and alkyl groups exert a weak electron-releasing inductive effect. A positive charge or unpaired electron is spread over a larger region. In a carbanion, alkyl donation pushes still more electron density onto an already negative carbon and destabilizes it; electron-withdrawing and resonance-accepting groups (carbonyl, nitrile, nitro) stabilize carbanions by dispersal.

Electrophiles and nucleophiles

An electrophile (“electron-pair loving”, despite acting as an acceptor) is electron-poor: H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br⁺ equivalents, BF₃, AlCl₃, carbocations and the δ+ carbon of a carbonyl or alkyl halide. A nucleophile has an electron pair available: OH⁻, CN⁻, halide ions, NH₃, H₂O, thiolates, carbanions and the π electrons of an alkene/arene. The curly arrow always starts at the nucleophile's electron pair (or a bond) and points to the electrophilic atom/bond — never the reverse.

Basicity and nucleophilicity are not synonyms. Basicity is an equilibrium affinity for a proton; nucleophilicity is a rate of attack at an electrophilic atom, often carbon. Solvent, size and polarizability matter. In protic solvents, larger and less strongly solvated I⁻ is generally more nucleophilic than F⁻ even though F⁻ is more basic. A bulky base such as tert-butoxide can remove a proton yet be a poor nucleophile at crowded carbon.

Inductive effect: a σ-bond tug that fades with distance

If X is more electronegative than carbon in C–X, the bonding electrons sit closer to X. That polarity is relayed weakly through adjacent σ bonds. Electron-withdrawing groups have a −I effect: –NO₂, –CN, –COOH, carbonyl groups and halogens, with halogen order F > Cl > Br > I. Electron-releasing alkyl groups have a modest +I effect relative to hydrogen, increasing roughly tert-butyl > isopropyl > ethyl > methyl. The effect is permanent but becomes small after about three bonds.

This explains carboxylic-acid strength. A −I substituent stabilizes the negatively charged carboxylate ion and pulls the acid equilibrium toward ionization. One chlorine near the acid increases strength, more chlorines increase it further, and moving chlorine farther away weakens the effect. Conversely, +I alkyl groups destabilize a nearby carboxylate slightly and make a carbocation slightly more stable.

Resonance: delocalization through a conjugated π system

Resonance appears when π electrons or a lone pair can overlap through adjacent p orbitals: π–π conjugation in butadiene/benzene, lone pair–π conjugation in phenoxide or an amide, and π–empty-p overlap in an allyl cation. Only electrons move in resonance drawings; atomic nuclei and σ frameworks stay fixed. Each drawing is a contributing structure, and the actual molecule is a lower-energy hybrid with fractional bond orders. Equivalent contributors contribute equally — acetate has two equivalent C–O bonds, benzene has six equal C–C bonds.

A group that donates π/lone-pair density into a conjugated system has a +R (or +M) effect: –NH₂, –OH, –OR and halogens (although halogens are simultaneously −I). A group that withdraws by π conjugation has a −R effect: –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR and –CO₂H when conjugated with the system. Resonance requires orbital alignment; twisting a π system out of coplanarity reduces it.

High-yield consequences are best read from the ion or molecule left after reaction:

  • Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because phenoxide is resonance-stabilized by the ring, whereas ethoxide localizes negative charge on oxygen.
  • Aniline is a weaker base than an alkylamine because nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring and less available to bind H⁺.
  • Carboxylate is stabilized by two equivalent resonance forms, one reason carboxylic acids are far more acidic than alcohols.
  • Amide nitrogen is weakly basic and the C–N bond has partial double-bond character because the nitrogen lone pair conjugates with C=O; this is the electronic basis of the planar peptide bond.
  • Allyl and benzyl cations/radicals disperse charge or spin over several carbons and form more readily than ordinary primary systems.
Effect Path Distance behaviour Needs π system? Classic readout
Inductive Through σ bonds Falls rapidly with each bond No Chloroacetic-acid strengths
Resonance Through overlapping p orbitals Can extend across the conjugated system Yes (or adjacent p/lone pair) Phenol acidity, aniline basicity
Hyperconjugation Neighbouring σ(C–H/C–C) → p/π* Immediate neighbour Needs adjacent p/π system Carbocation and alkene stability
Read intermediates by charge comfort

Positive centre? Ask what donates (+I, hyperconjugation, +R). Negative centre? Ask what withdraws or delocalizes (−I, −R). Radical? Donation and delocalization both help. That one question unlocks most order-of-stability items.

Common mistake

Five swaps the paper sets: lowest locants beat alphabetical order — number first for smallest locant set, then alphabetise prefixes; tautomerism is not resonance — tautomers move a proton and are distinct compounds in equilibrium, resonance moves only electrons within one compound; carbanion stability reverses the cation order because alkyl groups donate into an already negative carbon; inductive effects travel σ bonds and fade within a few carbons, resonance travels π systems across the whole molecule; and phenyl (C₆H₅) is not benzyl (C₆H₅CH₂) — one carbon's difference, a different compound family.

Chapter summary

  • Carbon's tetravalency, strong self-linking and multiple bonding create an enormous set of stable molecular architectures.
  • Functional groups and homologous series convert that diversity into learnable families; alkyl, aryl and benzyl must be distinguished by where the free valence lies.
  • Degree of unsaturation counts rings plus π bonds and is the fastest check before drawing or naming structures.
  • IUPAC names are built by seniority, parent selection, low-locant numbering and alphabetical assembly.
  • Structural isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers keep connectivity but differ in arrangement. E/Z, enantiomers, diastereomers, racemates and meso forms each answer a different question.
  • Homolysis makes radicals, heterolysis makes ions. Curly arrows track electron pairs from nucleophile to electrophile.
  • Alkyl donation and hyperconjugation stabilize carbocations/radicals but destabilize carbanions; resonance can dominate all three.
  • Inductive effects fade through σ bonds, while resonance operates only where p orbitals overlap; acid/base and intermediate-strength orders usually reveal which effect controls the system.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — four shared electron pairs complete carbon's octet in a neutral molecule.

2. (a) — strong C–C bonds allow chains, branches and rings.

3. (c) — phenyl is benzene minus one ring hydrogen.

4. (b) — benzyl's free valence is on the CH₂ next to the ring, so it is aralkyl rather than aryl.

5. (a) — one triple bond gives DU = 2 relative to an alkane.

6. (d) — the constant homologous increment is CH₂, 14 u.

7. (b) — replace the final -e of the parent hydride pattern appropriately: propan-2-ol.

8. (c) — for example CH₃CO₂H is ethanoic acid.

9. (b) — an alcohol and an ether share C₂H₆O but have different functional groups.

10. (a) — both are C₄H₁₀ alkanes, but the carbon skeleton changes from straight to branched.

11. (d) — only the –OH locant changes on the same four-carbon skeleton.

12. (c) — classic metamers are ethers/ketones/amines with different alkyl distribution around O, C=O or N.

13. (a) — proton shift is coupled to movement of unsaturation between C=O/C–C and C=C/C–O forms.

14. (c) — if either alkene carbon carries two identical substituents, exchanging sides gives the same molecule.

15. (b) — four different substituents normally remove symmetry at that tetrahedral centre.

16. (d) — equal enantiomers cancel optical rotation by external compensation.

17. (c) — each fragment receives one electron from the bond.

18. (b) — the atom taking both bonding electrons becomes anionic; the other becomes cationic.

19. (a) — electrophiles are Lewis-acidic electron-pair acceptors.

20. (d) — nucleophiles supply the pair used to form the new bond.

21. (b) — the empty p orbital is perpendicular to the plane of the three σ bonds.

22. (d) — a carbanion has an octet with a lone pair and behaves as a base/nucleophile.

23. (c) — σ polarization is relayed weakly and fades after a few bonds.

24. (a) — the nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing by both induction and resonance when conjugated.

25. (c) — nuclei and σ connectivity stay in place; only π/lone-pair placement changes among contributors.
